Ex came to me with a separation agreement that was a joke. I refused to sign it. Next we went to mediation, that was a waste of time. So we agreed to go to arbitration, but before that we submitted all the paperwork like the values of everything we had. Bank accounts, loans, pensions, vehicle values, had the house appraised, and got all the values of everything together.

Then we did a cross examination where our lawyers questioned each of us on what we did or didn't submit. Example: After we separated the ex got a new credit card and maxed it out in a couple months mostly on a trip to Vegas, and was trying to claim that it was marital debt and that I should have to pay it. Things like that.

Then we went to arbitration. During arbitration the arbitrator was taking notes while the lawyers spoke. My lawyer had everything drawn out and documented, but TONS were missed or ignored by the arbitrator. When I received the judgement I asked, "What about this? Where's that?" even though me and my lawyer presented evidence and documentation, it wasn't included. During the cross examination the values my ex had given were proven to be false, but the arbitrator used those values forgetting that they were proven to be lies or exaggerations (or the judge was just lazy and used the first numbers they found). My lawyer essentially said that the judgement is final and they couldn't do much about it.

My advice is this - Put in the time and effort and document and organize EVERYTHING. The value of everything. The arbitrator is going to be human, which means they're going to make mistakes and they're going to be lazy. Example: Your wife is going to take one vehicle and you're going to take the other vehicle - get a black book report for both with mileage for both and print them out. Give them to your lawyer and take them to the arbitration, and when the arbitrator is looking for the vehicle values they'll use your values because they're right there. Things like this.

Put in the time and effort!! How many hours do you have to work to make a few thousand dollars? 30, 50? 5 minutes of checking and printing off the value of something is a lot less than 50 hours. Put in the time and effort to document and organize everything. So that when the arbitrator has to look something up, they use your organized and easy to reference lists. And they're less likely to miss something if it's on your well documented lists.

My biggest regret during the arbitration process was that if I had just spent 5 minutes here, a couple hours there, I would have gotten thousands upon thousands of dollars for just a little bit of work. But I didn't put in the time to document and organize well enough. And don't rely on your lawyer to do it. Make sure you do it. Make sure you have it all documented and organized, for your lawyer.

Good Luck.

I'm only familiar with arbitration in a business dispute context, not family law. However, I can tell you I despise arbitration and try to never enter into agreements that do not provide for court trials of disputes unless I absolutely must.

The primary perceived benefits of arbitration over a court trial are lower expense and greater speed. There is definitely some truth to this. Court dockets can be fairly full and scheduling a trial can take longer. The expense issue, in my experience is much less true. You still have all the costs of discovery, deposing witnesses, lawyers writing complaints, answers, briefs, replies, et cetera.

What you do not have is extended motion practice which increases cost and schedule. However, extended motion practice is actually not very common in run of the mill disputes. It happens when really large sums are at stake or if both parties have lots of money and are willing to spend enormous amounts on lawyers in order to engage in procedural fighting, instead of substantive fighting.

The bad part of arbitration is that arbitrators are usually much more lax about applying judicial rules and precedent. Their decisions are also binding making them very hard to appeal in court. This is true even if they did something that could have been appealed if done by a judge in court. Now, court rules and binding precedent can cut both ways depending on your facts, but at least you are dealing with a much better defined and known set of rules, with a clear method for disputing their incorrect application.

You might consider mediation, but if that fails, I would strongly consider going to court over arbitration.
